expertNote.title: Test keyboard-only accessibility under constrained vision
expertNote.summary: A practical accessibility check is to use the operating-system voice assistant, restrict vision, and navigate the site or app by keyboard alone; an incorrect tab sequence can stop a disabled user completely.

evidenceSpans.text: Please put on some headphones, turn on the voice assistant of your OS, put on some blinders, and run your app or website… no mouse, just keyboard.
the second a tab is off, the person with a disability flies into a wall.

qualifiers: Based on regular accessibility work for the commenter’s company.

expertNote.title: AI-driven disclosure volume strains rclone security releases
expertNote.summary: The rclone maintainer reports a sharp increase in security disclosures, a substantial useful-signal rate, merge-management pressure, and much slower GitHub CVE assignment that forces releases to use CVE-PENDING entries.

evidenceSpans.text: In the first 10 years of the rclone project we received about 20 security disclosures through GitHub. We had to deal with over 40 in the last month!
The hit rate for those security disclosures is pretty good - about 75% of them have a nugget of something which needs looking at.

I was considering just merging the fixes straight to master just to make my life easier rather than holding a dozen independent security fixes on branches and merging them at the point release and hoping not to have too many conflicts to fix up. I've decided to stick with the process for the moment.
Before the AI apocalypse they took 2-3 days for an assignment but now it they are running at 3-4 weeks so I have to send the point releases out with CVE-PENDING in the changelog which isn't ideal.

qualifiers: First-hand report from an open-source maintainer.
Counts and delays describe the commenter’s current experience.

expertNote.title: GLM 5.3 balances capability, operability, and open-weight deployment
expertNote.summary: The commenter places GLM 5.3 slightly behind Kimi in capability but easier to run, expects better third-party price and speed, and says a 4-bit quantized copy can run locally on a 512 GB unified-memory Mac; they also favor its less restrictive behavior around cyber topics.

evidenceSpans.text: GLM 5.3 is probably the sweet spot open weights model if you want to go beyond deepseek flash or the new glm flash.
I used it with pi and had a fairly good time, especially since it’s less touchy about cyber and whatnot than the US guys.
It’s slightly behind Kimi in ability but it’s a lot easier to run it, I’d expect prices (and speed!) from third parties to be noticeably better.
Assuming you’re willing to drop a fat stack of cash on the upcoming Mac m5 ultra with 512 gb unified memory, you can even run it locally, quantized to 4 bit.

qualifiers: Local execution assumes 512 GB unified memory and 4-bit quantization.

expertNote.title: Dell reimbursed rejected Windows and bundled software licenses
expertNote.summary: A Dell E6420 buyer reports receiving a 143€ reimbursement after rejecting the Windows license terms, including roughly 50€ attributed to bundled antivirus and other software.

evidenceSpans.text: In 2011 I got a 143€ reimbursement from Dell for an E6420 laptop that I had bought for 910€.
I called the customer service, told the lady I did not agree with the Windows license terms
she just went "oh, ok, let me just edit a new invoice and wire you the money for Windows plus the Antivirus plus etc.".
I still got ~50€ for it on top of the OS license price.

expertNote.title: Suica feels faster than common contactless payment systems
expertNote.summary: A user reports that Suica completed full payment transactions in Japan with noticeably lower perceived latency than NFC, Apple Pay, tap-to-pay systems, Disney bands, and workplace badges.

evidenceSpans.text: If you haven’t experienced suica, it’s like magically fast.
Faster than NFC, faster than Apple Pay, faster than tap to pay, faster than Disney magic bands, faster than your work badge.
It absolutely floored me every time I used it in Japan and it’s a full payment transaction.

expertNote.title: Go, htmx, and SQLite form a simple responsive experiment stack
expertNote.summary: The commenter routinely starts experiments with Go, htmx, and SQLite because the combination stays simple and fast while still producing responsive applications.

evidenceSpans.text: Pretty much every experiment I build now starts with Go, htmx, and SQLite to keep things simple and fast but still responsive.

expertNote.title: Offline TVs can still trigger PC-side companion-app updates
expertNote.summary: The described behavior does not require the television to be online: connecting it to a Windows PC over HDMI or DisplayPort can trigger a companion-app update through Windows Update, and a hardware blocker can prevent that path.

evidenceSpans.text: The TV is completely offline.
They're talking about plugging the TV into a PC or laptop via HDMI or Displayport (like if you're running an HTPC), which then triggers a companion app update on the PC via Windows Update.
They then also discuss a hardware blocker for HDMI or DP to prevent this.

qualifiers: Correction of a common interpretation of the linked article.

expertNote.title: AWS documentation can obscure actionable account-linking steps
expertNote.summary: The commenter finds AWS documentation either too high-level or too verbose to be useful and cites linking AWS Partner Central with an AWS Management account as a painfully complicated example.

evidenceSpans.text: This is my experience with basically all of AWS documentation.

It is nearly always either (1) far too high-level to be of any actual use, or (2) far too verbose, with a massive volume of superfluous information I need to parse and discard before I get to the stuff I am trying to figure out.
I recently needed to link an AWS Partner Central account with an AWS Management account, and process and documentation was painfully complicated

expertNote.title: Example breadth in prompts can shape both model interpretation and human writing
expertNote.summary: The commenter found that supplying two examples followed by “etc.” discouraged language models from overfitting to the examples, then noticed that this prompting habit had transferred into their own everyday writing.

evidenceSpans.text: I had realized that I grown accustomed to this kind of language because, especially early on, LLMs would focus too much on the specific examples I'd provide when, really, I was just trying to give them a sense of what I was looking for.

I just picked up that providing two examples then adding the "etc." worked to get the LLM to not focus so much on the specific examples and to understand that they need to consider more than what I explicitly presented.
Of course, now I write like that in my social media comments, in Slack with my colleagues, etc. :>

qualifiers: First-hand observation rather than a controlled result.

division by zero bug in FFmpeg

expertNote.title: Consciousness, human concern, and moral patienthood are distinct concepts
expertNote.summary: The comment distinguishes subjective experience, human concern, and moral patienthood, then argues that the article misstates Descartes by conflating thinking, qualia, and the existence of a self with consciousness.

evidenceSpans.text: Whether or not something is conscious (has subjective experience) is independent of whether humans care about it.
Whether or not something is a moral patient (an entity worthy of consideration by moral agents) is independent of both human care and consciousness.
The cogito argument is about thinking, not qualia.
The subjective nature of qualia does not imply that they aren't real or that they're socially constructed.
He conflates the existence of a self with consciousness.

qualifiers: Philosophical distinctions and objections, not empirical findings.

expertNote.title: Narrow model-and-harness systems may replace all-purpose model ambitions
expertNote.summary: The commenter predicts that expensive general-purpose models aimed at inferring vague intent will give way to efficient, distilled and fine-tuned model-plus-harness systems designed for narrow, irregularly shaped tasks.

evidenceSpans.text: The infancy phase of this technology is represented by the pursuit of making wildly grand, wildly expensive, all-purpose models that somehow discern a user's full accurate intent from a lazy, underdeveloped, vague idea that they ambiguously and poorly express in a couple dozen words.

The adolescence will arrive as those outsized and ill-considered ambitions collapse and we instead see a cambrian explosion of restrained but efficient model+harness-tuples that have been distilled,  finetuned, and rigged to deliver on narrowly scoped but idiosyncratically-shaped tasks with incredible efficiency and erogonomics.

expertNote.title: US transfer friction increases reliance on payment intermediaries
expertNote.summary: The commenter contrasts simple QR-based bank payments outside the United States with US direct-transfer friction that makes services such as PayPal and Zelle more necessary.

evidenceSpans.text: Outside the US many banks offer simple QR payment options, the direct transfer difficulties US citizens encounter that make services like PayPal and Zelle necessary are entirely self imposed.

qualifiers: Broad regional comparison without named bank examples.

expertNote.title: Model distillation exposes tension in AI companies’ fair-use arguments
expertNote.summary: The commenter argues that treating book-to-model training as transformative is difficult to reconcile with opposing model-to-model distillation on fair-use grounds, especially when companies seek protection resembling the copyright claims they previously resisted.

evidenceSpans.text: It's ironic how AI companies are re-inventing their own form of privately enforced copyright, lobby the government to ban foreign competitors that don't respect it etc., all while spending the last 5 years fighting tooth and nail against the copyright of the training material they're using.

If you can take any book and turn it into a model, because it's "transformative enough", and "AI learns just like a person does", then surely a model distilling another model is transformative and fair use.

They tied themselves into knots fighting the letter of the law, and now, when they need the spirit of the law - that each creator deserves protection for their work - now we devolve to the law of the jungle.

qualifiers: Fair-use argument by the commenter, not verified legal advice.

expertNote.title: Accessibility improvements can benefit every website user
expertNote.summary: From prior university web-development work, the commenter consistently found that improving accessibility also improved the experience for users without disabilities.

evidenceSpans.text: I had to keep accessibility in mind a lot in my previous job (web development for a university).
The thing that I consistently found was that, the more accessible a website was, the better the experience for everyone, not just people with disabilities.

qualifiers: First-hand experience from university web development.

expertNote.title: Sanctioning infrastructure providers may expose users and developers to terrorism designations
expertNote.summary: The commenter warns that treating infrastructure providers as terrorists could create a precedent affecting users and developers of privacy, messaging, and cryptocurrency systems when radical groups use those systems.

evidenceSpans.text: this targeting of infrastructure providers as “terrorists” is unprecedented and concerning
If a radical group sets up shop on I2P, are I2P users and devs now terrorists?
What about Monero users/devs? Veilid? Tox? Signal?

qualifiers: Policy-risk analogy rather than a confirmed technical effect.

expertNote.title: Grid isolation does not change a generator’s environmental impact
expertNote.summary: The comment states that the Clean Air Act Acid Rain Program excludes power generators disconnected from the public grid, then objects that grid connectivity is unrelated to environmental impact.

evidenceSpans.text: > Clean Air Act (CAA) Acid Rain Program (ARP) does not apply to power generation facilities that are not connected to a public electricity grid, commonly referred to as “islanded” power generation facilities.
This of course makes no sense whatever, as whether or not a power generator is connected to the grid has nothing to do with its environmental impact.

qualifiers: The regulatory-scope claim is quoted in the comment.

expertNote.title: App-gating browser-capable features can drive users away
expertNote.summary: A user says forcing browser-capable functions behind an app causes them to abandon those functions or the site entirely, reducing engagement, because app privacy and security risks outweigh the value of installation.

evidenceSpans.text: If you're going to needlessly gate certain functions behind an app that work on a desktop browser (or could work in-browser), then I just won't use those functions.
If by extension that degrades the value I get from your site, then I just won't use the site, and I won't be contributing to ADU stats you promote to advertisers.
Every single company has turned this into a situation where I cannot trust your apps with privacy or security, and the risk and hassle isn't worth the install.

qualifiers: A single user’s stated behavior and trust concerns.
